intro: Painswick's churchyard is the reason most people stop in this Cotswold village. Around a hundred yews, clipped every September into rounded and pom-pom shapes, line the paths to St Mary's among a collection of chest tombs that starts in the early 17th century. Legend fixes the number at 99, because the Devil is said to kill any hundredth, and the count has never quite settled. The churchyard is open and free, and the Cotswold Way runs through the village.
meta_description: Legend says Painswick churchyard can only hold 99 yews. About a hundred clipped yews, their disputed count, their planting date and the September trim.
question_meta: How many yews are in Painswick churchyard? Legend says 99, the V&A counted 103, and the church plan shows 100. How old they are and when they are clipped.
question_answer: Painswick churchyard holds about a hundred clipped yews. Legend says there are 99 because the Devil destroys any hundredth, a hundredth was planted in 2000, the Victoria and Albert Museum once counted 103 and the church plan shows 100. Most were planted in the early 18th century, according to the National Trail.
question_context: The yews of St Mary's are not ancient trees but an ancient habit. The National Trail dates most of them to the early 18th century, about 300 years ago, while another account puts the planting in the 1790s, and the sources do not settle which is right. What has continued without a break is the clipping. Every September the yews are cut back into their rounded and pom-pom shapes, and more than two tons of clippings are collected each year. Fresh yew clippings are a source of paclitaxel, a drug used in cancer treatment. The number is the famous part. Folklore holds that only 99 yews will ever grow here, because the Devil will destroy a hundredth. In 2000, when parishes across the Diocese of Gloucester were given yews to mark the millennium, Painswick planted a hundredth. Counts since vary, from the church plan's 100 to the 103 recorded by the Victoria and Albert Museum, and the National Trail says more than 100. The Ancient Yew Group calls the churchyard an exceptional site. Count them yourself.

faq.q: When are the Painswick yews clipped?
faq.a: Every September, according to the National Trail. More than two tons of clippings are collected each year.

faq.q: How do I get to Painswick without a car?
faq.a: Stagecoach buses run from Stroud in about 20 minutes. Stroud station is about 6 km away, and the Cotswold Way passes through the village.

trees.name: The clipped yews of St Mary's, Painswick

location.address: St Mary's Church, Churchyard, Painswick, Gloucestershire GL6 6SU

trees.story:
Painswick's churchyard is supposed to hold 99 yews, because legend says the Devil will kill any hundredth. The parish has tested it. In 2000, when parishes in the Diocese of Gloucester were given yews for the millennium, a hundredth went in. The Victoria and Albert Museum once counted 103, and the church's own plan shows 100. Nobody agrees on the number, so we will not give you one. Call it about a hundred and count them yourself.

They are not ancient. The National Trail says most were planted in the early 18th century, roughly 300 years ago, while another account puts them in the 1790s. Either way they share the ground with a collection of chest tombs that begins in the early 17th century.

What makes the place is the scissors. Every September the yews are clipped back into rounded and pom-pom shapes along the path to the tower, and more than two tons of clippings are collected each year. Fresh yew clippings are a source of paclitaxel, a drug used in cancer treatment, so the trim has a second life.

The Ancient Yew Group calls it an exceptional site. It is the opposite of a single veteran trunk. It is a whole churchyard of yews, roughly three centuries old and trimmed like a hedge.
trees.access: Open churchyard (Ancient Yew Group lists access as public; church parochial church council ground). Free, no opening hours.
trees.transport: In the centre of Painswick village; the Cotswold Way passes through. Stagecoach buses from Stroud (about 20 minutes); nearest station Stroud, about 6 km.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the clipped yews, about a hundred of them, trimmed into rounded and pom-pom shapes along the paths among the chest tombs. They line the path to the tower of St Mary's.
trees.verify_notes: Compact ensemble, one place to stand (the churchyard), treated as one collectible point; not a single ancient trunk. AYG (Tim Hills, 18 Feb 2007; site 'Notable'): 'An exceptional site with its 100 or so yews clipped into an assortment of shapes', with a collection of chest tombs from the early 17th century onwards; no girth data. National Trail page: most yews planted in the early 18th century (about 300 years old); the 100th yew was planted in 2000 when parishes in the Diocese of Gloucester were given yews for the millennium; legend says 99 and the Devil would destroy a hundredth; page also says 'more than 100 trees'; clipped each September, over 2 tons of clippings collected for processing (fresh yew clippings are a source of the drug paclitaxel). Wikipedia: folklore 99, V&A counted 103, church leaflet plan shows 100; count unsettled, so do not state one number. CONFLICT on date: National Trail says early 18th century; a church (Beacon Benefice) page seen only in a search summary gave the 1790s, not fetched (403), so unconfirmed. Alive: AYG record 2007 plus clipped yearly (National Trail). No register girth; the 'ancient' label does not apply. Position: AYG grid SO86650963 converted, approximate.
